Ezra 1.summary: In his first year, the LORD stirs up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, and he proclaims that the LORD has charged him to build a house at Jerusalem (Ezra 1:1–2). Any of God's people may go up, and their neighbors are to help them with silver, gold, goods, and beasts (Ezra 1:3–4). The leaders of Judah and Benjamin, the priests, and the Levites rise up to go, "with all them whose spirit God had raised" (Ezra 1:5–6). Cyrus brings out the vessels Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple, and Mithredath the treasurer counts them out to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah (Ezra 1:7–11).
Ezra 1.whereWeAre: 2 Chronicles ended with Jerusalem burned and Cyrus king of Persia inviting God's people to go home. Ezra begins with the same decree, as God stirs up Cyrus and the first exiles prepare to leave Babylon. Chapter 2 lists the families who return.

keyFigures.name: Cyrus
keyFigures.role: King of Persia, whose spirit the LORD stirs to send the exiles home.

keyFigures.name: The leaders of Judah and Benjamin
keyFigures.role: Rise up with the priests and Levites to go and build.

keyFigures.name: Mithredath
keyFigures.role: The treasurer who counts out the temple vessels.

keyFigures.name: Sheshbazzar
keyFigures.role: The prince of Judah, who carries the vessels to Jerusalem.

keyThemes.explanation: The return fulfills the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah.
The LORD stirs up the spirit of a pagan king to send his people home.
Those whose spirit God raised up choose to make the long journey.

Ezra 2.summary: The chapter lists the people who return with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, family by family and town by town (Ezra 2:1–35). It also lists the priests, Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants (Ezra 2:36–58). Some cannot show their family records, and the governor says those priests must not eat the most holy things until a priest stands up "with Urim and with Thummim" (Ezra 2:59–63). The whole company is 42,360, plus 7,337 servants and 200 singers (Ezra 2:64–67). Some family leaders give freely for the house of God, and everyone settles in their own towns (Ezra 2:68–70).
Ezra 2.whereWeAre: Cyrus let the exiles go home in chapter 1. This chapter lists the families who return with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, 42,360 in all, and the priests who cannot prove their family line. In chapter 3 they rebuild the altar in Jerusalem.

keyFigures.name: Zerubbabel
keyFigures.role: Leads the first return from Babylon.

keyFigures.name: Jeshua
keyFigures.role: The priest who returns with Zerubbabel.

keyFigures.name: The Tirshatha
keyFigures.role: The governor, who keeps priests without records from the most holy things.

keyFigures.name: The chief of the fathers
keyFigures.role: Family leaders who give freely to rebuild the house of God.

keyThemes.explanation: The careful list shows that God's people return as real families from real towns.
Priests who cannot prove their line must wait before serving.
Family leaders give gold and silver so the house of God can be rebuilt.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Both preserve lists of the returning exiles, although some names and figures vary.

Ezra 3.summary: In the seventh month the people gather "as one man" to Jerusalem, and Jeshua and Zerubbabel build the altar and offer burnt offerings, though they fear the peoples around them (Ezra 3:1–3). They keep the feast of tabernacles and the daily offerings, even before the temple's foundation is laid (Ezra 3:4–6). They pay masons and carpenters and bring cedar from Lebanon by sea to Joppa (Ezra 3:7). In the second year the foundation is laid, and the priests and Levites praise the LORD, "because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel" (Ezra 3:8–11). Old men who had seen the first house weep aloud while others shout for joy, and no one can tell the sounds apart (Ezra 3:12–13).
Ezra 3.whereWeAre: The returning families were listed in chapter 2. Now they rebuild the altar, keep the feast of tabernacles, and lay the temple's foundation, as some shout for joy and the old men weep. Chapter 4 tells how their neighbors stop the work.

keyFigures.name: Jeshua son of Jozadak
keyFigures.role: Leads the priests in building the altar.

keyFigures.name: Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel
keyFigures.role: Leads the people in rebuilding the altar and the foundation.

keyFigures.name: The priests and Levites
keyFigures.role: Praise the LORD with trumpets, cymbals, and song.

keyFigures.name: The ancient men
keyFigures.role: Older priests, Levites, and fathers who had seen the first house and weep.

keyThemes.explanation: The people rebuild the altar and offer sacrifices before the temple stands.
At the foundation they sing that God's mercy endures for ever.
Shouts of joy and the weeping of old men rise together.

Ezra 4.summary: The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin offer to help build, but Zerubbabel and Jeshua answer, "Ye have nothing to do with us to build an house unto our God" (Ezra 4:1–3). The people of the land weaken the builders' hands and hire counsellors against them through the reign of Cyrus until Darius (Ezra 4:4–5). The chapter then gathers later accusations: Rehum and Shimshai write to Artaxerxes that Jerusalem is "the rebellious and the bad city" (Ezra 4:6–16). Artaxerxes searches the records and orders the building of the city stopped, and the officials force the Jews to cease (Ezra 4:17–23). The temple work stops until the second year of Darius (Ezra 4:24).
Ezra 4.whereWeAre: The temple foundation was laid in chapter 3. Now the people of the land offer to help, are refused, and then work against the builders, and letters to Persian kings bring the work to a stop. In chapter 5 the prophets Haggai and Zechariah get it moving again.

keyFigures.name: Zerubbabel and Jeshua
keyFigures.role: Refuse the adversaries' offer to build with them.

keyFigures.name: The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin
keyFigures.role: Offer to help, then work to stop the building.

keyFigures.name: Rehum and Shimshai
keyFigures.role: The chancellor and scribe who accuse Jerusalem in a letter.

keyFigures.name: Artaxerxes
keyFigures.role: King of Persia, who orders the building of the city stopped.

keyThemes.explanation: The leaders refuse outside help and build only as Cyrus commanded them.
Enemies use fear, hired counsellors, and letters to stop God's work.
The work stands still for years until God moves again.

Ezra 5.summary: The prophets Haggai and Zechariah prophesy to the Jews, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin to build again, "and with them were the prophets of God helping them" (Ezra 5:1–2). Tatnai the governor and Shetharboznai ask who commanded the building, but they cannot stop it, for "the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews" (Ezra 5:3–5). Their letter to Darius reports the elders' answer: they are servants of the God of heaven, rebuilding the house Nebuchadnezzar destroyed (Ezra 5:6–12). The elders say Cyrus decreed the rebuilding and returned the vessels by Sheshbazzar, and the letter asks Darius to search the king's treasure house (Ezra 5:13–17).
Ezra 5.whereWeAre: Opposition stopped the temple work in chapter 4. Now Haggai and Zechariah stir the people to build again, and the governor Tatnai writes to King Darius to ask who allowed it. Chapter 6 gives Darius' answer.

keyFigures.name: Haggai and Zechariah
keyFigures.role: Prophets who stir the people and help them build.

keyFigures.name: Zerubbabel and Jeshua
keyFigures.role: Begin to build the house of God again.

keyFigures.name: Tatnai
keyFigures.role: Governor on this side the river, who asks who allowed the work.

keyFigures.name: The elders of the Jews
keyFigures.role: Answer that they serve the God of heaven and earth.

keyFigures.name: Darius
keyFigures.role: King of Persia, to whom the letter is sent.

keyThemes.explanation: Haggai and Zechariah's preaching gets the people building again.
The eye of God on the elders keeps the work from being stopped.
The elders admit their fathers' sin and tell why the temple fell.

Ezra 6.summary: Darius has the records searched, and a roll with Cyrus' decree is found at Achmetha (Ezra 6:1–5). Darius tells Tatnai to let the work alone and to pay its costs from the king's taxes, and he warns that anyone who changes the order will be hanged on a beam from his own house (Ezra 6:6–12). The elders build and prosper through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah, and the house is finished on the third day of Adar in Darius' sixth year (Ezra 6:13–15). They dedicate it with joy, offer twelve he goats for all Israel, and set the priests and Levites in their courses (Ezra 6:16–18). The returned exiles keep the Passover and the feast of unleavened bread seven days with joy (Ezra 6:19–22).
Ezra 6.whereWeAre: Tatnai asked Darius to search the royal records in chapter 5. The search finds Cyrus' decree, Darius orders the work paid for, and the temple is finished and dedicated with a joyful Passover. Then the story jumps ahead nearly sixty years to Ezra himself in chapter 7.

keyFigures.name: Darius
keyFigures.role: Finds Cyrus' decree and orders the temple built at the king's cost.

keyFigures.name: Tatnai
keyFigures.role: The governor, who obeys the king's order quickly.

keyFigures.name: The elders of the Jews
keyFigures.role: Finish the temple through the prophets' encouragement.

keyFigures.name: Haggai and Zechariah
keyFigures.role: Prophets whose words help the work prosper.

keyFigures.name: The children of the captivity
keyFigures.role: Dedicate the house and keep the Passover with joy.

keyThemes.explanation: The officials who questioned the work are told to pay for it.
The temple is completed by God's command and the kings' decrees.
The people dedicate the house and keep the Passover with joy.

Ezra 7.summary: In the reign of Artaxerxes, Ezra, a priest descended from Aaron and "a ready scribe in the law of Moses," goes up from Babylon (Ezra 7:1–6). He arrives in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the king's seventh year, for he "had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach" (Ezra 7:7–10). Artaxerxes' letter lets any Israelite go with him, sends silver and gold for offerings, and frees temple workers from taxes (Ezra 7:11–24). It also tells Ezra to appoint judges who know God's law and to teach those who do not (Ezra 7:25–26). Ezra blesses the LORD for putting this in the king's heart and gathers leaders of Israel to go with him (Ezra 7:27–28).
Ezra 7.whereWeAre: The temple was finished in chapter 6. Now, years later, Ezra the scribe comes from Babylon with a letter from King Artaxerxes, because he "had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD" (Ezra 7:10). Chapter 8 tells of his journey.

keyFigures.name: Ezra
keyFigures.role: A priest and scribe who goes to Jerusalem to teach God's law.

keyFigures.name: Artaxerxes
keyFigures.role: King of Persia, who sends Ezra with gifts and authority.

keyThemes.explanation: Ezra prepares his heart to seek God's law, to obey it, and to teach it.
The king grants Ezra's request because God's hand is upon him.
Ezra blesses God for putting kindness in the king's heart.

Ezra 8.summary: Ezra lists the family heads who go up with him from Babylon (Ezra 8:1–14). At the river of Ahava he finds no Levites, so he sends to Iddo at Casiphia, and "by the good hand of our God upon us" Levites and Nethinims come (Ezra 8:15–20). Ezra proclaims a fast, because he is ashamed to ask the king for soldiers after saying God's hand is on those who seek him (Ezra 8:21–23). He weighs the silver, gold, and vessels out to twelve chief priests and tells them, "Ye are holy unto the LORD; the vessels are holy also" (Ezra 8:24–30). God keeps them from enemies on the way, the treasure is weighed again in the temple, and the returned exiles offer burnt offerings (Ezra 8:31–36).
Ezra 8.whereWeAre: Artaxerxes sent Ezra to Jerusalem with gifts and authority in chapter 7. Now Ezra gathers Levites, fasts for a safe journey without soldiers, and brings the treasure safely to the temple. In chapter 9 he learns of a grave sin among the people.

keyFigures.name: Ezra
keyFigures.role: Gathers the travelers, calls a fast, and weighs out the treasure.

keyFigures.name: Iddo
keyFigures.role: The chief at Casiphia, who sends Levites and Nethinims.

keyFigures.name: Sherebiah and Hashabiah
keyFigures.role: Levites who join the journey and help carry the treasure.

keyFigures.name: Meremoth
keyFigures.role: The priest who weighs the treasure in the house of God.

keyThemes.explanation: Ezra seeks a safe way by fasting and prayer, and God answers.
Ezra will not ask for soldiers after telling the king that God protects those who seek him.
The treasure is weighed before and after the trip so all is kept honestly.

Ezra 9.summary: The princes tell Ezra that the people, priests, and Levites have married daughters of the peoples of the lands, and that leaders have led the way (Ezra 9:1–2). Ezra tears his clothes, plucks hair from his head and beard, and sits stunned until the evening sacrifice, while those who tremble at God's words gather to him (Ezra 9:3–4). He falls on his knees and prays, "O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee" (Ezra 9:5–7). He thanks God for "a little reviving in our bondage" and admits God has "punished us less than our iniquities deserve" (Ezra 9:8–13). He ends by confessing, "we cannot stand before thee because of this" (Ezra 9:14–15).
Ezra 9.whereWeAre: Ezra arrived safely in Jerusalem in chapter 8. Now leaders tell him that many, even priests and Levites, have married women of the nations around them, and Ezra prays a prayer of confession. Chapter 10 shows how the people respond.

keyFigures.name: The princes
keyFigures.role: Report to Ezra that the people have married foreign wives.

keyFigures.name: Ezra
keyFigures.role: Mourns and confesses the people's sin before God.

keyFigures.name: Those who tremble at God's words
keyFigures.role: Gather around Ezra in his grief.

keyThemes.explanation: Ezra is so troubled by the people's sin that he sits stunned until evening.
Ezra says "our iniquities," counting himself with the guilty.
God has punished them less than they deserve and left them a remnant.

Ezra 10.summary: As Ezra weeps before the house of God, a great crowd gathers, and Shechaniah says, "yet now there is hope in Israel concerning this thing" (Ezra 10:1–2). He proposes a covenant to put away the foreign wives and their children, and Ezra makes the leaders swear to do it (Ezra 10:3–5). Ezra fasts, and a proclamation calls all the exiles to Jerusalem within three days (Ezra 10:6–8). On the twentieth day of the ninth month the men sit in the street in the great rain, and they answer Ezra, "As thou hast said, so must we do" (Ezra 10:9–12). Because it is raining and the matter is large, they ask that each case be handled by rulers and the elders and judges of each city (Ezra 10:13–17). The book ends with a list of the priests, Levites, and other men who had taken foreign wives (Ezra 10:18–44).
Ezra 10.whereWeAre: Ezra confessed the people's sin in chapter 9. Now the people gather in the rain, agree to put away their foreign wives, and the book ends with a list of the men involved. The story continues in Nehemiah 1, where Nehemiah hears that Jerusalem's walls are still broken down.

keyFigures.name: Ezra
keyFigures.role: Prays, fasts, and calls the people to separate from their foreign wives.

keyFigures.name: Shechaniah
keyFigures.role: Son of Jehiel, who confesses the sin and proposes a covenant.

keyFigures.name: The men of Judah and Benjamin
keyFigures.role: Gather in the rain and agree to Ezra's word.

keyFigures.name: Jonathan and Jahaziah
keyFigures.role: Named in Ezra 10:15 in connection with the plan; the Hebrew word can mean they stood for it or against it.

keyThemes.explanation: Shechaniah says there is still hope for Israel if they turn back.
The whole assembly agrees to do as Ezra says.
The people ask that each case be heard carefully, city by city.
The book closes with the names of those involved and the children affected.
